sections.title: 1 Frequency Support from Electric Vehicles for
sections.text:
Advancing Renewable Energy Integration
Dilip Pandit, Student Member, Atri Bera, Member, Tu Nguyen, Senior Member, Raymond Byrne, Fellow,
Babu Chalamala, Fellow, John Pierre, Fellow, Dongliang Duan, Senior Member, Nga Nguyen, Member, IEEE
Abstract—The integration of renewable energy resources
(RERs) in the modern power grid is increasing rapidly because
of aggressive decarbonization goals, lower costs, and increased
government investment. However, higher penetrations of inverter-
based generation can lead to frequency stability issues because
of reduced system inertia. This paper develops a framework for
quantifying the contribution of electric vehicles (EVs) toward
providing frequency support to the grid and thus increasing the
penetration limit of renewable energy resources (RERs). EVs
are considered to provide both inertial response and primary
frequency response support to the grid. A stochastic approach
incorporating the uncertainties associated with the behavior of
EVs is developed to derive the discharge limit of EV aggregators.
A multi-machine system frequency response (MM-SFR) model is
developed, which incorporates the dynamic virtual inertia and
droop coefficients of EV aggregators derived from the EV control
modules. Frequency security constraints are developed from
this MM-SFR model, which, along with the converter voltage
security and low voltage ride-through constraints, are integrated
within a nonlinear optimization framework to determine the
RER integration limit. The efficacy of the proposed approach
is validated using the RTS-GMLC test system.
Index Terms —Electric vehicles, frequency security, inertia
response, renewable energy resources, voltage security.

sections.title: I NTRODUCTION
sections.text:
A. Background
Propelled by low-carbon energy policies, low costs of oper-
ation, and the goal of phasing out fossil fuels, the modern grid
is experiencing rapid integration of renewable energy resources
(RERs). The increasing penetration of RERs by replacement
of conventional generation can lead to increased frequency
stability issues in the grid due to their intermittent and low-
inertia characteristics [1]. This issue may lead to system
operators curtailing RER generation and planners investing
in less RER-based generation, thus delaying the transition
to a decarbonized grid. A potential solution to this problem
can be utilizing EVs to provide frequency support to the
grid. The integration of EVs has been increasing globally and
is projected to increase from 30 million in 2022 to about
240 million in 2030 [2]. EVs are capable of charging and
discharging at high power levels to provide inertia support
to the grid. This capability is being enhanced as the power
electronic converters of EVs improve. This makes EVs good
candidates for providing frequency support to the grid, leading
to increased penetration of RERs and thus accelerating the
transition to a decarbonized future.
B. Relevant Literature & Research Gaps
The contribution of EVs toward frequency stability using
virtual inertia has been investigated extensively in recent years.
Among the different techniques used to extract frequency
support from EVs, a popular approach is the inclusion of
EVs in the system load frequency control (LFC) model.
Plug-in EVs are included in the LFC model using derivative
control-based inertia emulators with tunable gain parameters
in the approaches developed in [3], [4]. Another widely
used approach for virtual inertia emulation is using different
control strategies to generate converter switching signals for
the primary converter in grid-to-vehicle connections [5], [6].
Recently, model predictive control has been used in virtual
inertia emulation due to its robustness under RER uncertainties
[7], [8]. In addition to the inertia response (IR) based on
system RoCoF, EVs can also support the grid in the frequency
recovery phase. Primary frequency response (PFR) using EVs
can be achieved using a droop gain parameter controlling
the amount of EV power injection after the V2G aggregators
determine the discharging/charging limits [9]–[12]. Research
in [9], [10] propose models for EVs to provide primary
frequency support under contingencies whereas [11], [12]
illustrate the potential frequency support from EVs in real-
world grids. The aforementioned works that model the IR and
PFR support from EVs deploy simulation models to assess the
frequency response. While the simulation-based models can
capture diverse operational characteristics, they are unsuitable
for planning analysis, where simulations are performed over
large time horizons and require solving optimization problems.
Along with accurate modeling of system frequency dynam-
ics under EV integration, a significant interest of the research
community lies in leveraging the frequency support capabili-
ties of EVs and converter-based generation to enhance RER
penetration. The simulation-based models mentioned above
mostly focus on assessing the frequency response with IR and
PFR support from EVs but do not assess the contribution of
EVs on the integration limit of RERs. References [13]–[16]
propose approaches to directly evaluate the integration limits
of RERs and RER-based microgrids in bulk power systems
with respect to the system frequency response. These works,
however, do not incorporate the frequency support from EVs
or other converter-based generators into their models.
Frequency security-constrained stochastic unit commitment
(FSCUC) frameworks proposed in [17]–[19] incorporate the
frequency support from converter-based resources using the
multi-machine system frequency response model. They model
the IR from converter-based resources using the virtual syn-
chronous machine control, while the PFR is modeled using
the droop control. Also, these works implicitly enforce a limit
on RER integration using the frequency security constraints.
However, these studies deploy constant values for virtual iner-
tia and droop gains, which leads to an overestimated support
from converter-based generation under large disturbances [20].
Recent works in [20], [21] implement virtual inertia param-
eters dependent on the unit-commitment decision variables
while [22], [23] deploy variable droop gain parameters in
their FSCUC models to incorporate the frequency support
from converter-based generation more accurately. These works
either only consider the IR [20], [21] or only the PFR [20],
[21] from converter-based resources in their FSCUC models.
In addition, while the works mentioned consider various
aspects of frequency support from converter-based resources,
they do not consider the voltage stability or security constraints
on the converter interface. This is a major drawback of existing
literature since the step disturbances considered for frequency
stability analysis are typically accompanied by voltage sags at
the converter point of connection. To ensure converter stabil-
ity under reduced grid voltage, the converters must readjust
the active and reactive power setpoints [24]. The readjusted
setpoints affect the frequency support from converter-based

sections.title: 3 resources and should be considered while estimating the RER
sections.text:
penetration limits. The research in [25]–[27] addresses the
issue of steady-state voltage stability by incorporating the
static voltage stability constraints and optimizing the active
and reactive power outputs of converter-based resources as
decision variables in the FSCUC framework. However, the
stability constraints in [25]–[27] are limited to steady-state and
do not ensure converter stability and low voltage ride-through
(LVRT) compliance under grid voltage sags. In addition, none
of the works mentioned incorporate EV aggregators as a po-
tential converter-based resource in their FSCUC formulations.

sections.title: Summary of Contributions
sections.text:
This paper develops a framework that not only quantifies
the frequency support from EVs but also derives an optimiza-
tion framework for calculating RER penetration limits and
demonstrates how frequency support from EVs can enable
increased RER penetration. The contribution of EVs to system
inertia and regulation is modeled using a modified multi-
machine system frequency response (MM-SFR) model. The
virtual inertia and droop gain of the EV aggregators are
modeled as decision variables, and their expressions in terms
of the RER integration limit are derived using the control
modules for IR and PFR support. The penetration limit of
RERs is then obtained using a non-linear programming (NLP)
optimization framework that incorporates the AC power flow
constraints in addition to the IR and PFR support constraints
of EV aggregators, frequency security constraints, converter
voltage security, and LVRT constraints formulated using the
requirements set forth by the IEEE-Standard 2800-2022 [28].
Dynamic simulations, 24-hour dispatches, and large time-
horizon stochastic simulations are performed to demonstrate
the efficacy of the proposed approach. The major contributions
of the paper are listed as follows:
1) Developing an improved MM-SFR model that incorporates
frequency support from plug-in EVs using dynamic virtual
inertia and droop control of EV aggregators. We derive
expressions for the EV inertia and droop parameters in
terms of the RER penetration limit, IR, and PFR control
parameters and deploy them into the MM-SFR model to
obtain the revised frequency security constraints.
2) Formulating a NLP framework to determine the maxi-
mum penetration limit of RERs while incorporating the
frequency support capabilities of EV aggregators. The
framework is comprehensive as it considers the ACOPF
constraints, IR and PFR constraints of EV aggregators,
converter voltage security constraints, and LVRT con-
straints while evaluating the frequency support from EV
aggregators. Existing literature considers a subset of these
constraints while evaluating the RER penetration limit.
3) Developing a stochastic approach to quantify the discharge
capacity of EV aggregators for providing frequency sup-
port, a step not within the scope of existing works that
consider frequency support from converter-based genera-
tion. The proposed approach uses probabilistic techniques
to aggregate the charge and discharge characteristics of
individual EVs and derives the discharge limits of EV
aggregators.
D. Organization
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section

sections.title: presents the MM-SFR model incorporating frequency sup-
sections.text:
port from EVs along with the models for IR and PFR support
from EVs. Section III presents the random sampling approach
to determine the total number of connected EVs. Section IV
develops the converter voltage security criterion. Section V
develops a NLP framework to determine the RER penetration
limit. It is followed by simulation and results in section VI
and conclusion in section VII.

sections.title: D ISCHARGE CAPACITY OF EV A GGREGATORS
sections.text:
In this work, we consider the plug-in EVs to have Vehicle-
to-Grid (V2G) technology. V2G enables EVs to respond
rapidly to frequency fluctuations by feeding surplus power
into the grid or drawing power as needed [8]. With V2G, the
EVs are equipped with bidirectional chargers, allowing them
to charge from the grid and discharge power back into it. In
addition to V2G, while considering frequency support from a
massive number of EVs, it is paramount to model the actual
number of EVs participating in frequency support. If all the
EVs in the system are assumed to participate in frequency
regulation at any time step, the frequency support from EVs
is significantly overestimated. Hence, in this work, only the
EVs that are already at the charging stations are assumed to
be able to provide frequency support. To model the number
of EVs present at the charging stations and eligible to provide
frequency support, we have developed a stochastic procedure
in Algorithm 1. For each EV , the cumulative density function
of the EV SoC at the charging start time extracted from
[31] is compared against a random number from the uniform
distribution. Then, depending on the operation modes of EVs,
the actual number of EVs at the charging station, their charging
load, and their discharge capability for frequency support are
estimated. For EVs not at the charging station, their traveling
distance is randomly assigned using the NHTS database [32].

In the above formulation, objective (27) minimizes the load
curtailment while simultaneously minimizing the generator
fuel costs. The ESS charging and discharging costs c−
s , c+

are set such that ESS charge when the system generation is
surplus and discharge when the total generation cannot cater
to the system demand. Equations (28c) and (28d) enforce
the equality constraints for nodal active and reactive power
balance. Equations (28e) and (28f) denote the limits for load
curtailment and node voltages. The transmission line limit
constraint is enforced using equation (28g), while the generator
limits are enforced using equations (28h)-(28k). The lower
limits of conventional generators are relaxed to avoid integer
variables in the NLP, which is a common procedure for solving
ACOPF in planning problems [33]. It should also be noted
that the generator and transmission line limits depend on their
forced outage status ug,t and uij,t, which are determined and
deployed during the stochastic simulations. The ESS operation
constraints are enforced using equations (28l)-(28n).
In this paper, the RER limit is enforced using a linear
constraint in equation (28o) that emphasizes that the RERs can
only account for a certain percentage of system demand during
time t. The value of βt is majorly determined by the frequency
security constraints in equations (28p), (28q), and (28r), which
correspond to the maximum RoCoF, QSS frequency, and
frequency nadir constraints, respectively. Depending on the
outage statistics, a capacity flow model is solved to obtain
the values of γg,t, which are subsequently used to determine
DCV
t , HCV
t , RT
t , FT
t . Details of the capacity flow model is
present in reference [34]. The capacity flow model is solved as
a workaround for introducing integer variables within the NLP.
Integer variables convert the NLP into a mixed-integer NLP
(MINLP), significantly increasing computation times. While
the optimization framework tries to minimize the value of βt
to minimize the fuel costs, the frequency security constraints
impose a limit on the reduction of βt, resulting in a dispatch
that is frequency secure.
The eth EV aggregator’s contribution to frequency response
is modeled using the setpoint active power and the EV inertia
and droop reciprocals. The expression for the EV inertia
constant given by equation (12) is expressed as constraints in
(28s) and (28t). Similarly, the QSS and frequency nadir droop
reciprocals in (17) and (19) are enforced using constraints
(28u), (28v), and (28w). Using the expression for the critical
voltage for converter stability from (25), constraint (28x) is
formulated. Based on the grid voltage reduction ∆Ve, the
power setpoints are controlled such that the critical operating
voltage for the converter remains does not exceed Ve,t − ∆Ve.
The aggregator’s power setpoints are dependent on the grid
voltage Ve,t at the node where the aggregator is connected.
It can also be noticed that the grid voltage Ve,t is a decision
variable whose steady-state limits are enforced using constraint
(28f). The active and reactive power setpoints for the convert-
ers are further constrained by the hourly discharge limit for
the aggregator P EV
e,t , obtained using equation (21). The LVRT
constraints for EV aggregators are enforced as equation (28z).
In this paper, for simplicity, the function T in constraint (28z)
is approximated by a quadratic polynomial fit of the minimum
ride-through times in Fig. 7.

sections.title: S IMULATION AND RESULTS
sections.text:
The efficacy of the proposed approach is demonstrated
using the RTS-GMLC test system [35]. This system is well
suited for this work since it is one of the few available test
systems that incorporate RERs, including PV , wind, concen-
trated solar power (CSP), hydro, and also ESSs. The RER
resource database consists of day-ahead forecasts recorded at
hourly intervals for a year. The generation mix consists of 74
conventional generation units, 20 hydro units, 25 PV farms,
31 roof-top PV ,1 CSP, 4 winds farms, and one ESS. There are
73 nodes distributed among three regions. Each area consists
of distributed loads with a peak of 2850 MW.
The EV aggregator is assumed to be present in bus 313
of the RTS-GMLC system since the particular bus already
includes an ESS. The traveling patterns of EV users are
extracted using the national household travel survey (NHTS)
database [32]. The total aggregated EV power for IR and
PFR at each hour is obtained using Algorithm 1. This work
considers high EV integration scenario with the total number
of EV users being 100,000. Each EV has a battery with a
rated charging/discharging capacity of 15 kW and an energy
capacity of 60 kWh. Efficiencies for ESSs, individual EVs,
and EV aggregators are taken as 0.85.
The generator inertia, fraction of power from high-pressure
turbines, droop, and damping coefficient are extracted using
the procedure in reference [36]. The maximum RoCoF values
obtained in this paper are evaluated considering a 50 ms time
delay of the RoCoF relay [30]. The NLP is solved using the
IPOPT solver in pyomo [37]. The frequency security limits
considered in this work are derived from Table 1 of the NERC
standard BAL-003-1 for ERCOT, USA [38], and they are
implemented as follows:
• Disturbance size ( ∆Pt): The disturbance size is assumed
to vary at all simulation hours, and it is considered to be
10% of the load demand during that hour. This disturbance
size during peak demand roughly translates to the N-2
criterion for RTS-GMLC system, which is also the resource
contingency criterion in BAL-003-1.
• Frequency nadir limits (∆f lim): It is set as 0.7 Hz according
to the prevailing under-frequency load shedding (UFLS)
limit in BAL-003-1 for ERCOT.
• RoCof limits (
    d f
dτ
   
lim
): As reported by reference [39], under
critical inertia, it takes 0.416 seconds for ERCOT’s fre-
quency to decrease from 59.7 Hz to 59.3 Hz, corresponding
to the RoCoF of 0.96 Hz/s. To ensure that the system inertia
remains above critical inertia, 0.96 is taken as the RoCoF
limit in this work.
• QSS frequency limit ( ∆f ss,lim): It is set as 50% of the
frequency nadir limit.
A. Validation of the modified MM-SFR model
First, we have compared the performance of our proposed
MM-SFR-based analytical model with IR and PFR constraints
against the baseline simulation-based model and the virtual
10
synchronous machine (VSM)-based models in the literature.
Three models are formulated as follows:
• Case I: The baseline model illustrated in Fig. 8 is simulated
in MATLAB/Simulink and is used. The EV IR and PFR
modules are directly incorporated with the base MMSFR
model. This model considers filtering time constants and
saturation blocks of IR and PFR modules. The IR gain
KEV
e = 2 and rated droop REV
e = 0.01 are used.
• Case II: The VSM strategy proposed in references [17]–
[19] for emulating the frequency support of converter-based
resources is integrated with the MMSFR model. Static
values of virtual inertia constant (evaluated using (9)) and
rated droop coefficient are used.
• Case III: Proposed MMSFR model with IR and PFR con-
straints is deployed. We use equations (12), (17), and (19) to
dynamically update the inertia and droop reciprocals based
on the varying disturbance sizes.

It is due to the fact that the virtual inertia and droop values

The proposed analytical model in case III successfully models

These observations demonstrate that the proposed model can

tractable to be included in the NLP framework.

The following can be observed from Fig. 11:
• In case I, Fig. 11a shows that the system experiences
frequency nadir violations in multiple hours. This is because
the system dispatch prioritizes RER integration due to the
low production cost associated with these resources, as
evident with the largest RER power for cases I in Fig.
11b. This causes the inertia, regulation, and other parameters
from conventional generators to reach low values, affecting
the frequency nadir. This effect is minimized in case II
where the RER integration limits are enforced. Using the
RER integration factors in Fig. 11c, the RER penetration
in the system is limited to satisfy the frequency nadir
constraint. It should be mentioned that there is a minor nadir
limit violation in hour 21 of case II. This is due to the linear
constraint approximating the RER integration limit in (28o).
• The contribution of EVs in promoting the RER integration
is illustrated by the case III plots in Fig. 11. When the
frequency support from EVs is incorporated, the system
experiences higher penetration of RERs between hours 5-

case II. As seen in Fig. 11c, there is a significant reduction
in βt for case III during hours 5-16 compared to case II,
contributing to larger RER power in Fig. 11b.
• Case IV illustrates the impacts of imposing the converter
voltage security constraints on the RER penetration limit.
As expected, when the voltage of the bus connected to
the aggregated EVs drops to Ve,t − ∆Ve, the active and
reactive power setpoints are readjusted in proportion to the
voltage drop. The reduced active power setpoint affects the
frequency support from the EV aggregators and causes the
system to impose heavier restrictions on the penetration of
RERs to ensure frequency security. Due to this, the RER
penetration is smaller in case IV compared to case III. This
is also evident in Fig. 12 where the RER integration factor
increases with increased ∆Ve. Neglecting the converter
voltage security constraint causes an overestimation of the
frequency support from energy storage devices in case III,
leading to an optimistic estimation of the RER penetration
limit. The proposed approach addresses this issue by in-
cluding the voltage security constraint while determining
the RER penetration limit.

Since the proposed NLP is non-linear and non-convex,
the solution quality of the 24-hour dispatches generated by
the NLP is analyzed using the overall unscaled NLP error
in Fig. 13. The overall NLP error is the maximum among
primal infeasibility (constraint violation), dual infeasibility,
and complementarity, details of which are present in [40].
The NLP is solved using the overall error tolerance of 1e−4.
However, the figure shows that the NLP errors are significantly
smaller than the tolerance in all simulation hours, indicating
that the problem constraints and optimality conditions are
clearly satisfied. In addition, we also tested the possible
global convergence of the algorithm with the “multistart”
solver with “midpoint guess and bound” strategy. With 1000

sections.title: System Frequency Response and RER Penetration with
sections.text:
Stochastic Simulations
In this section, stochastic simulations are performed to as-
sess the RER penetration under different simulation scenarios.
Stochastic simulations capture a vast range of uncertainties
introduced by the random generator and transmission line
outages, RER inputs, and EV user charging/discharging char-
acteristics. We simulate 1000 sample paths for cases I-IV , with
one sample path performing a yearly simulation. Within a
sample path, the procedure in Algorithm 1 is initially run
to obtain the EV aggregator load and discharge capability.
Then, within the hourly simulation, the next event approach
is used to simulate the forced outages of generators and
transmission lines. Details of the next event approach are
present in reference [34]. The RER integration and frequency
security indices obtained from the NLP dispatch are recorded
over all the simulation hours and sample paths.
Initially, the cumulative distributions of frequency security
indices are presented in Fig. 14. Maximum RoCoF, frequency
nadir, and QSS frequency limits are violated with a much
higher probability for case I when the RER integration limit is
not considered. In addition, the violations are extremely severe,
up to three times the safety limit. In cases II-IV , the RER
limits imposed prevent the frequency nadir and QSS frequency
from reaching extreme values, while some values violate the
safe limits due to the multiple forced outages of generators.
The IR and PFR support from the EV aggregator reduces the
probability of violating the safe limits in case III compared
to case II, as they can provide frequency support during the
forced outages of generators. However, the converter voltage
security constraints undermine the frequency support from
the EV aggregator, resulting in slightly increased frequency
security violations in case IV compared to case III. This is
illustrated by the case IV curves being slightly lower than the
case III curves in Fig. 14.
Table I illustrates the impacts of imposing the RER inte-
gration limit constraint. In case II, the total energy over the
simulation year from RERs reduces significantly compared to
case I. It is because the only way for case II to keep the
frequency security constraints within limits is by curtailing
the RER power and increasing the number of conventional
generators online. However, when frequency support from

D. Discussion
Simulation results show that the proposed method can
estimate the RER penetration limit in power grids while
incorporating frequency support from EVs. Initially, the dy-
namic simulations illustrated the importance of the proposed
dynamic virtual inertia and droop coefficients, especially un-
der increased RER penetration. One-day dispatch simulations
highlighted the efficacy of the proposed NLP in limiting the
RER integration to satisfy the frequency security constraints.
The simulations also highlighted how the frequency support
from EVs can elevate the RER penetration in the system
without compromising frequency security. Stochastic simu-
lations highlighted the system frequency security and RER
penetration under random forced outages of system generators.
The key benefit of the proposed NLP framework is that it
is computationally inexpensive and suitable for use in plan-
ning frameworks. This is primarily attributed to the approach
not requiring integer decision variables, removing the need
to solve a MINLP problem. Regarding the applicability of
the proposed framework in real-world, as mentioned in the
ACOPF white paper issued by FERC in reference [41], “The
ACOPF problem must be solved weekly in 8 hours, daily
in 2 hours, hourly in 15 minutes, every five minutes in 1
minute and for self-healing post-contingency in 30 seconds.”
The computation times reported in Table I illustrate that the
proposed NLP adheres to these limits for very short periods
(such as 5-minute dispatch) and planning problems (hourly
resolution). In this work, we have primarily focused on solving
the NLP hourly within a stochastic simulation to determine
the RER penetration in the system. However, the computation
times in Table I indicate the applicability of the NLP for
shorter time scales.

sections.title: C ONCLUSION
sections.text:
This paper formulates an improved approach to incorporate
frequency support of EVs to promote RER integration. The
contribution of EV aggregators to system frequency response
is modeled using the dynamic virtual inertia and droop coef-
ficients, which in turn are determined using the IR and PFR
control modules. The resulting EV aggregator parameters are
then deployed in the modified multi-machine system frequency
response (MM-SFR) model to obtain the frequency security
indices. To determine the discharge limits of EV aggregators
for frequency support, a stochastic framework is developed.
A non-linear optimization framework is then devised to deter-
mine the maximum penetration limit of RERs in the system.
The framework incorporates frequency security constraints,
IR and PFR constraints of EV aggregators, converter voltage
security, and LVRT constraints. Simulation results on the
IEEE RTS-GMLC illustrate that the proposed framework
incorporates the IR and PFR contribution of EVs and improves
the system frequency response and RER integration while
also illustrating the importance of considering voltage secu-
rity constraints. The proposed model can be used in system
planning studies such as reliability analysis since the method
does not require simulation models. Computation times show
that the model can also help system operators determine the
RER penetration limits in near real-time with changes in EV
penetration and system demand.
